Group nearby sites into sampling units

Source: R/coverage.R
group_sites.Rd

Merges sites within a given distance of each other into one sampling unit, summing counts and efforts. Grouping helps when single sites lack some habitats or hold too few individuals, at the cost of fewer units.

Usage

group_sites(
  data,
  site,
  lon,
  lat,
  radius_km,
  linkage = "complete",
  species = NULL,
  habitat,
  abundance,
  effort = NULL
)

Arguments

data

Long-format data: one row per species x site x habitat.

lon, lat

Names of the longitude and latitude columns (decimal degrees; one location per site).

radius_km

Grouping radius in km: one number, or a named vector with one radius per species.

linkage

"complete" or "single".

species, site, habitat, abundance, effort

Long format: names of the columns holding species (optional; without it the data are one species), site (or other replicate), habitat, abundance (counts) and sampling effort (optional; without it every row has effort 1).

Value

A tibble in long format with the original column names: the species (if given), site (the group name), habitat, abundance and effort (named "effort" if there was no effort column), plus lon and lat (mean of the sites) and n_sites (number of sites merged). Every sampled group x habitat appears for every species, with 0 where the species was not recorded.

Details

Sites are clustered by complete linkage on great-circle distance, so every pair of sites in a group lies within radius_km of each other (single linkage, linkage = "single", can chain distant sites together). With radius_km = 0 only sites with identical coordinates are merged.

Counts are summed over the sites of a group, and so are efforts: the effort of a group in a habitat is the summed effort of the sites that sampled that habitat. Without an effort column, every site x habitat has effort 1, so the group's effort is the number of sites that sampled the habitat. Groups are named after their sites (joined with "+").

The radius is not chosen automatically: choosing it to maximise completeness or niche breadth would be circular. Use radius_sensitivity() to see how the number of units, their completeness and the niche breadth estimates change with the radius.

See also

radius_sensitivity(), check_coverage()

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- simulate_isodars(1.5, 1.5, 5, 5, n = 12, format = "long")
sites <- unique(d$site)
xy <- data.frame(site = sites, lon = stats::runif(12, 0, 0.05),
                 lat = stats::runif(12, 0, 0.05))
d <- merge(d[c("site", "habitat", "abundance")], xy)
g <- group_sites(d, site = "site", lon = "lon", lat = "lat", radius_km = 2,
                 habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
head(g)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   site               habitat abundance effort    lon    lat n_sites
#>   <chr>              <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>   <int>
#> 1 site1+site12       hab1           25      2 0.0438 0.0168       2
#> 2 site1+site12       hab2           49      2 0.0438 0.0168       2
#> 3 site1+site12       hab3           85      2 0.0438 0.0168       2
#> 4 site10+site5+site8 hab1           51      3 0.0382 0.0423       3
#> 5 site10+site5+site8 hab2           93      3 0.0382 0.0423       3
#> 6 site10+site5+site8 hab3          152      3 0.0382 0.0423       3
